Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones
Medical equipment such as needles or drips

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try to push them out of my mind

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
I have permanently changed for the worse
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Weapons): Weapons or objects used as weapons
issues.explanation: For trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, weapon-related visual triggers are hard to reconcile unless there is additional unreported violent trauma. Hospital smells and loss-related conversations fit, but weapons/object-as-weapon cues are clinically implausible for the same index trauma.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'You can never know who will harm you' implies interpersonal danger/assailant threat, which is poorly matched to the validated trauma of a child's serious illness. This also aligns awkwardly with the rest of the profile, which is otherwise illness/loss/moral injury themed rather than assault-based.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: 'Intense rage on recall' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile for an 80-year-old mother traumatized by a child's life-threatening illness. The other items center on helplessness, permanent change, loss-related and hospital triggers, and intrusive affect without image. Distress, fear, guilt, grief, or sadness would fit more coherently; rage is not impossible, but here it is insufficiently supported by any corresponding appraisal or trigger content and stands out as clinically incongruent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Face Hiding: cover face with hands
issues.explanation: 'Cover face with hands' is not well supported as a maladaptive strategy in this profile. The active formulation links maladaptive strategies mainly to negative appraisals and memory, and the other strategies chosen (avoid going out, thought suppression) fit intrusive distress and negative beliefs. Face hiding is more typical of acute shame/panic/social exposure and is not clearly connected to the hospital/loss triggers, intrusive memory pattern, or appraisals provided, making it the least coherent item in this set.

vignette: Layla was forty-eight when her son, Tariq, was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit with a sudden, unexplained respiratory failure. The hospital corridors were cold, and the air carried the sharp, unwavering sting of antiseptic cleaners. She remembers the sight of the IV poles, the coiled tubing, and the needles that punctured his skin day after day, each one a tiny invasion that she could only watch. When the monitors changed rhythm, when the attending physicians spoke in quiet, measured tones about losing someone, Layla found herself gripping the edge of the plastic chair until her knuckles ached. The illness raged for eleven days. By the time Tariq was discharged, fragile but breathing, Layla had already learned that the world could turn without warning. In the weeks and months that followed, certain moments would catch her entirely off guard. A colleague casually mentioning that their father had passed would send a heavy, familiar weight into her chest, though she never had a clear picture of the ICU room when the feeling hit. Sometimes the grief arrived fully formed, a wave of sorrow so sudden and overwhelming that she would pause mid-sentence and press her palms to her eyes until it passed. When the emotion would surface, she tried to push it out of her mind, repeating routine tasks to drown it out, but the memory had a way of forcing its way in when she was least prepared. To keep it at bay, she began to avoid places where the antiseptic scent might linger, steering clear of neighborhood clinics and the distant wail of approaching ambulances. She told herself it was simply prudent, that she did not need to put herself through the same dread. As a community social worker, Layla's days usually involved home visits and office appointments, but her avoidance quickly took root in her workplace. She would decline referrals involving critically ill children or chronic hospitalizations, telling her supervisor that she needed to focus on administrative files instead. During team meetings, she would shift her chair away from the medical supply cabinet, uncomfortable with the visual presence of tubing and syringes, and she stopped volunteering for bereavement support groups after hearing a client describe the long goodbye of a dying parent. She had come to believe that her role as a caregiver had not protected her when it mattered most. She questioned whether she had made the right choices at the bedside, convinced she had acted in ways that went against her deepest values. What frightened her most was not the grief itself, but the certainty that she had been permanently altered, that the capable, grounded woman she used to be was gone. She felt utterly powerless to stop bad things from happening to anyone, including herself, no matter how carefully she tried to plan or prepare. The habit of staying home grew heavier over the years. What began as avoiding medical centers slowly turned into a reluctance to leave her apartment unless absolutely necessary, leaving her professional relationships to fray and her caseload to stagnate. She missed the work, but the fear of bumping into medical equipment or hearing a conversation about loss felt insurmountable. Eventually, the isolation wore thinner than her resolve. During a routine check-up where the nurse adjusted an IV line nearby, Layla's breath caught, and the old, unbidden grief rose again, sharper than before. It was that moment that finally brought her to seek professional support. She did not want to be ruled by avoidance or haunted by sudden sorrow, but rather hoped she might finally find a way to sit with the weight of what happened, trusting that she might step back into the world she loved without bracing for the next blow.
